<reason>PRO built a narrow, consistent rule (upfront authorization for defined uses, fresh permission only for unpurchased material synthetic alterations) and defended it steadily without overreach, answering both pressure questions directly with A1/A2 and giving a workable materiality standard. CON was sharper and more vivid, landing real hits on "who decides materiality, and when" and the boilerplate-consent prediction, but its case had internal tension: it conceded the refused-line case is a real wrong (leaning on contract law) while its two remaining harms—an editing-room chokepoint and consent collapsing into click-through—partly cancel each other out (if consent becomes boilerplate, the chokepoint largely dissolves). PRO's closing weighing—that even imperfect consent leaves performers with more protection than deleting the requirement, and that silence should not default to consent for a new synthetic performance—was a clean answer that CON never fully defeated; CON's "launders costs" line was memorable but speculative. Two clipped CON turns also cost execution. Competitive, but PRO's route to victory survived more intact.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B4.1]/[B4.4]-[B4.5] sequence—conceding the refused line as a wrong already covered by contract law, then turning PRO's "reasonable viewer / courts resolve disputes" answer into "a judge, after release" and predicting boilerplate consent—was the most damaging exchange; PRO's closing partially blunted it by arguing that a default consent requirement still beats no requirement even under unequal bargaining.</best_rebuttal>
